rules.label: First days back
rules.text: Phase conditioning in: about half the volume in week 1, work-to-rest at least 1:4, acclimatize to heat over 7-14 days.

rules.label: Confusion while exercising in heat
rules.text: Treat as exertional heat stroke: stop, 911, cold-water immersion now; cool first, transport second.

rules.label: Cooling goal
rules.text: 38.9 C or less within 30 minutes of collapse, then out of the tub and to hospital.

sources.cite: NSCA Certification Handbook: CSCS detailed content outline (Scientific Foundations; Practical/Applied: program design, exercise technique, program implementation, organization and administration)
sources.note: Relayed from the course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/fitness.ts, read 2026-10-08), not re-read for this case. The objective titles are the course's own words.

sources.cite: Caterisano A, Decker D, Snyder B, et al. CSCCa and NSCA Joint Consensus Guidelines for Transition Periods: Safe Return to Training Following Inactivity. Strength Cond J. 2019;41(3)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes (first 100,000 of 127,339 characters): after 2 weeks or more of inactivity, conditioning 'phased in gradually and progressively'; the 50/30/20/10 rule (returning athletes at least 50% less volume in week 1 and 30% less in week 2; new athletes 50, 30, 20, 10% over four weeks); weight training work-to-rest 1:4 or more in week 1, 1:3 in week 2, at least 1:2 after; no more than 3 days of weight training in the first week; heat acclimatization over 7-14 days, exertional heat stroke cooled to 38.9 C (102 F) or less within 30 minutes of collapse, cold-water immersion fastest; sickle cell trait raises the risk of collapse and sudden death; exertional rhabdomyolysis mostly follows 'a novel workout regimen', especially after detraining, and 'Athletes who develop the symptoms associated with ER need to be quickly admitted to the hospital'.

sources.cite: NSCA. Inter-Association Task Force for Preventing Sudden Death in Collegiate Conditioning Sessions (introduction page, May 2017; citing Casa DJ, et al. J Athl Train. 2012;47(4))
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch; only the introduction was on the page: the leading causes of conditioning deaths are exertional sickling with sickle cell trait, exertional heat stroke and cardiac conditions; workouts 'too novel, too much, too soon, or too intense' are linked to exertional rhabdomyolysis; 11 of 21 deaths were on day 1 or 2. The full recommendations were not read.

sources.cite: NASEMSO. National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, Version 3.0 (March 2022): Hyperthermia/Heat Exposure
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the full text Iowa HHS hosts (https://hhs.iowa.gov/media/198/download) through summarizing fetches with quotes; NASEMSO's own page, read the same day, still presents Version 3 (2022) as current and names no later version. Heat stroke is told from heat exhaustion by altered consciousness, seizures or coma when no thermometer is available; rapid cooling takes priority over other interventions such as monitoring or IV access; 'Ice bath immersion provides the most rapid cooling mechanism'; cool until below 39 C (102.2 F), or until mental status improves when temperature cannot be measured; truncal ice packs are less effective than evaporation; do not use wet cloths that 'may trap heat'; every patient with life-threatening heat illness is transported.

His core temperature at collapse (41.2 C), how fast it climbs untreated in the sun and how fast each method cools him (cold-water immersion about 0.2 C a minute, wet ice towels 0.06, shade and a fan 0.03) are authored FLAG figures in the order the sources give: immersion is the fastest method, and the goal is 38.9 C or less within 30 minutes of collapse. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

brief.situation: You are the strength and conditioning coach for a college soccer team. Today is the first team conditioning session after five weeks off, at 4 pm, 32 C and humid.
handover: The athletic trainer is on the next field with a radio and measures core temperature; the coach starts first aid and runs the emergency action plan.
An ice-water tub is in the equipment shed.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes.
The screen shows the client, your read-outs and findings, the plan and the rules that apply now.
When you end the session you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident record: what you planned and why, what you saw, and how he was cooled and handed over.

parts.label: Planning
parts.criteria: First day back after five weeks in high heat: about half volume, work-to-rest 1:4, water breaks, heat-policy changes, and a cold-water tub set up before the session.
parts.modelAnswer: After five weeks off, in the policy's high heat category, I ran a transition day: half volume, 1:4 work-to-rest, water every 15 minutes, with the ice tub ready by the field.

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Confusion or odd behavior while exercising in heat is exertional heat stroke until proven otherwise; sweating does not rule it out.
parts.modelAnswer: He became confused and ran the wrong way in the heat: exertional heat stroke until shown otherwise, even though he was still sweating.

parts.label: Cool first, transport second
parts.criteria: 911 and the athletic trainer at once; cold-water immersion within minutes; out at about 38.9 C (the athletic trainer's rectal reading) within 30 minutes of collapse; then hand over to EMS; never drive him away hot.
parts.modelAnswer: 911 and the athletic trainer at once; into the ice tub within a minute; out at 38.9 C on the athletic trainer's rectal reading, inside 30 minutes; then to the paramedics with the times.

source.note: Exercise stopped within 2 minutes of a warning sign; a teaching figure, as for the physical therapy profile.

expertPath.text: Check the heat policy; a transition day at half volume, 1:4 work-to-rest, water breaks; the ice tub filled and set up.
Confused in the heat: stop him, 911 and the athletic trainer, into the tub within a minute.
The athletic trainer's rectal readings; out at about 38.9 C, inside 30 minutes; hand over to the paramedics with the times.

cooledFirst.headline: Cool first, transport second
cooledFirst.body: A day-one plan that respects five weeks off and the heat, a tub ready before anyone ran, and immersion within a minute of the confusion. That is how heat stroke ends with a full recovery.

cooledLate.headline: He recovered, with gaps
cooledLate.body: Check the day-one plan (half volume, 1:4), whether the tub was ready, and how fast immersion started.

hotTransport.headline: Never drive heat stroke away hot
hotTransport.body: Cooling on site comes first; immersion to about 38.9 C, then transport.

organInjury.headline: Thirty minutes is the window
organInjury.body: Shade, a fan and towels cool far too slowly. Immersion is the fastest method, and the tub should be waiting before the session starts.

scoring.modelReasoning: First day back after five weeks, in high heat: phase in conditioning (about half volume, work-to-rest 1:4, water breaks, heat-policy changes) and set up the ice tub beforehand. Confusion while exercising in heat is exertional heat stroke until shown otherwise: stop him, activate the emergency plan (911 and the athletic trainer), and immerse him in ice water within minutes; cool to about 38.9 C on the athletic trainer's rectal reading within 30 minutes of collapse, then hand over to EMS. Cool first, transport second; never drive him away hot.
